segments.text: This is Maya, who runs Packaging Line Four: nineteen machines moving toward one shift target, with plenty that can change along the way.

Her real challenge isn't more data; it's that alarms, production, quality, and maintenance sit in different systems — so answers used to arrive in the next-morning report, long after the recovery call.

That is why her day starts in the control tower, where those systems come together on Databricks, in one governed live view — letting her follow the line as a whole instead of piecing the shift together screen by screen.
At eleven forty-seven, Filler Three stops and downstream machines begin to starve; each OEE point is worth about three hundred thousand euros a year, so Maya has minutes to make the recovery call.
Maya asks exactly that, in the same language she would use with her team: can we still hit the shift target?
The copilot reads the live line state, carries that context forward, and hands the problem to the right specialist from a whole roster built for the line.
Behind the scenes, it runs real solvers, testing the plan against a thousand scenarios of speed, overtime, and CIP timing — not just guessing.
The recommendation returns with assumptions, cost, and trade-offs in view, so Maya can review the plan — and approve it.
On the roadmap, MCP connections carry approved work orders, holds, and schedule updates into the systems that own them.
As the filler comes back online, the control tower closes the loop, showing the line recover in real time.
That is ProdLine CoPilot: one connected picture, clearer options, and Maya still firmly in control.
